record.original_question: Develop reliable and easy-to-use numerical software for Painlevé equations that improves on generic Runge–Kutta-type ODE solvers by exploiting the integrable structure of these equations, in particular their formulation through isomonodromy and associated Riemann–Hilbert problems, and determine whether integrable discretizations should be used as part of such numerical methods.

evidence.quote: Ideally what is needed is reliable, easy to use software to compute numerically the solutions of the Painlev´e equations.
The Runge–Kutta method, and variants, are standard ODE solvers. Can we do better for integrable equations such as the Painlev´e equations?

Painlev´e equations are "integrable" and solvable by the isomonodromy method through an associated Riemann–Hilbert problem. How can we use this in the development of software for studying the Painlev´e equations numerically?

It is well known that there are discrete Painlev´e equations, which are integrable discrete equations that tend to the associated Painlev´e equations in an appropriate continuum limit. Should we use a "integrable discretization" of the Painlev´e equations?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
The six Painlevé equations P_I, P_II, P_III, P_IV, P_V, P_VI are a distinguished list of second-order nonlinear ordinary differential equations of the form w'' = F(z, w, w'), where F is rational in w and w' and locally analytic in z, characterized by the Painlevé property that all movable singularities of their solutions are poles. Their generic solutions, the Painlevé transcendents, define nonlinear special functions. Each Painlevé equation admits an isomonodromic Lax pair: solutions correspond to monodromy-preserving deformations of an associated linear system, and the Cauchy problem can be linearized through a Riemann–Hilbert problem on a contour in the complex plane with prescribed jump matrices determined by Stokes data. Each Painlevé equation also has integrable discrete analogues (the discrete Painlevé equations), which are integrable difference/q-difference equations whose continuum limits recover the Painlevé equations.

Problem: Design a reliable, easy-to-use numerical method (and supporting software) for computing solutions of the Painlevé equations that improves on generic adaptive Runge–Kutta-type ODE integrators by exploiting the integrable structure of these equations. Specifically:

(a) Develop and analyze a numerical scheme based on the isomonodromy formulation that computes a Painlevé transcendent at a point z by numerically solving the associated Riemann–Hilbert problem with prescribed Stokes/monodromy data, providing rigorous error bounds, robust handling of the movable poles, and uniform accuracy across the complex plane (including near critical points and along Stokes rays).

(b) Determine whether using an integrable discretization (a discrete Painlevé equation that has the given continuous Painlevé equation as a continuum limit) as the underlying time-stepping scheme yields provable advantages—such as preservation of geometric/integrable structure, improved stability near poles, or better long-range accuracy—over standard non-structure-preserving ODE solvers, and either construct such an integrable-discretization-based solver with quantitative comparison to Runge–Kutta methods, or rule out asymptotic advantages.
artifact.status_search_result: Partial progress exists: Olver and Trogdon developed spectrally accurate numerical schemes for the Riemann–Hilbert problems associated with Painlevé II and related integrable systems, demonstrating that the isomonodromy/RH approach can outperform standard ODE solvers, especially near poles. However, a comprehensive, reliable, and easy-to-use software suite covering all six Painlevé equations uniformly across the complex plane, along with a definitive comparative assessment of integrable discretizations as solvers, has not been fully achieved.

status_evidence.title: Numerical Solution of Riemann–Hilbert Problems: Painlevé II
status_evidence.snippet: A spectrally accurate method for solving matrix-valued Riemann–Hilbert problems numerically, with effectiveness demonstrated by computing solutions to the homogeneous Painlevé II equation.
status_evidence.claim: Riemann–Hilbert based numerical methods for Painlevé II have been developed, showing the isomonodromy approach is computationally viable.

status_evidence.title: Painlevé Equations — Nonlinear Special Functions (Clarkson)
status_evidence.snippet: Solutions to Painlevé II are inherently unstable; small perturbations cause oscillations and poles which break standard ODE initial value problem solvers.
status_evidence.claim: Standard ODE solvers struggle with Painlevé transcendents, motivating structure-exploiting numerical methods that remain to be fully developed.
